- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

input.prompt:
Search this repository very thoroughly for any rate-limiting middleware — per-user or otherwise. Look for:
1. Files or code referencing "rate limit", "rateLimit", "rate-limit", "throttle", "throttling"
2. Any middleware registration that limits API requests
3. Any configuration of request limits (e.g., requests per minute/hour/second)
4. Dependencies like express-rate-limit, rate-limiter-flexible, or similar packages

Search across all file types including JS, TS, Python, config files, package.json, etc. Report what you find — file paths, line numbers, and the actual limit values if any exist.

content.text:
Here are my findings from a thorough search of the repository.

---

**This repository does NOT have any rate-limiting middleware for API requests.** There is no per-user, per-IP, or global rate limiter that limits the number of HTTP/gRPC/Connect requests a client can make over a time window (e.g., requests per minute/hour/second).

Here is the detailed breakdown:

## What was searched

1. All source files (Go, TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, JSON, YAML, proto, etc.) for terms: `rate limit`, `rateLimit`, `rate_limit`, `throttle`, `throttling`
2. Go module dependencies (`go.mod`, `go.sum`) for rate-limiting packages (e.g., `golang.org/x/time/rate`, `rate-limiter-flexible`, etc.)
3. Frontend dependencies (`web/package.json`) for packages like `express-rate-limit`, `bottleneck`, `p-throttle`
4. HTTP status code 429 ("Too Many Requests") and gRPC `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` error returns
5. All middleware/interceptor registrations in the server stack
6. Login brute-force protection or lockout mechanisms
7. Reverse proxy or Docker/Nginx configurations

## What was found (no request-rate limiting)

### 1. Server middleware stack (no rate limiter registered)
File `/bench/home/work/server/server.go` (lines 51-52) registers exactly two middleware on the Echo server:
- `middleware.Recover()` -- panic recovery
- `newCORSMiddleware(profile)` -- CORS headers

### 2. Connect/gRPC interceptor chain (no rate limiter)
File `/bench/home/work/server/router/api/v1/v1.go` (lines 133-138) registers four interceptors:
- `MetadataInterceptor` -- converts HTTP headers to gRPC metadata
- `LoggingInterceptor` -- request logging
- `RecoveryInterceptor` -- panic recovery
- `AuthInterceptor` -- authentication/authorization

None of these is a rate limiter.

### 3. Concurrency limiters (NOT rate limiters)
There are semaphore-based concurrency limits for resource-intensive operations, but these are NOT rate limiters -- they limit how many operations run simultaneously, not how many requests a user can make per time period:

- `/bench/home/work/server/router/api/v1/v1.go` lines 39-41, 59-60: `thumbnailSemaphore` limited to **3 concurrent** thumbnail generations; `imageProcessingSemaphore` limited to **2 concurrent** image processing operations.
- `/bench/home/work/server/router/fileserver/fileserver.go` lines 45-46, 116: `maxConcurrentThumbnails = 3` using a semaphore.

### 4. Request body size limit (NOT a rate limiter)
File `/bench/home/work/server/router/api/v1/v1.go` line 20: `maxAPIRequestBytes = 256 << 20` (256 MB). This caps the size of individual request bodies via `http.MaxBytesHandler`, not the number of requests.

### 5. Content/upload size limits from protobuf settings
File `/bench/home/work/proto/store/instance_setting.proto` lines 90, 112-113: `upload_size_limit_mb` and `content_length_limit` are instance-level settings for upload/content sizes, not request-rate limits.

### 6. Email rate limiting -- documentation only, NOT implemented
File `/bench/home/work/internal/email/doc.go` line 86 mentions "Rate limit email sending to prevent abuse" as a security recommendation in a comment. File `/bench/home/work/internal/email/README.md` lines 286-297 shows a code example for rate limiting emails using `golang.org/x/time/rate`, but this is documentation/example code only -- it is not actually implemented in the email package's source code.

### 7. No rate-limiting dependencies
- `go.mod`/`go.sum`: No `golang.org/x/time/rate` or any third-party rate-limiting library is imported.
- `web/package.json`: No `express-rate-limit`, `rate-limiter-flexible`, `bottleneck`, `p-throttle`, or similar packages.

### 8. No login brute-force protection
The auth service (`/bench/home/work/server/router/api/v1/auth_service.go`, `/bench/home/work/server/router/api/v1/auth_service_session.go`) does not track failed login attempts or implement account lockout/cooldown mechanisms.

## Summary

This codebase has **zero rate-limiting middleware** for API requests. There is no protection against:
- Brute-force login attempts
- API abuse / denial-of-service from excessive requests
- Per-user or per-IP request quotas

The only request-related limits are:
- A **256 MB request body size** cap
- **Concurrency semaphores** (3 concurrent thumbnail jobs, 2 concurrent image processing jobs) to prevent memory exhaustion
- Instance-configurable **upload size** limits
